boards-phd:linkedin:4482462486.desc: Introduction Are you interested in the communication networks behind modern AI systems? Would you like to combine mathematical modeling with experiments on programmable network hardware to make AI infrastructure faster and more energy-efficient? In this PhD project, you will develop models and orchestration methods for the networks that connect GPUs during large language model inference. Are you our next PhD candidate in high-performance AI networking? Job Description Your research challenge Large language models rely on powerful computing infrastructure to generate responses. When inference […] requirements, complemented by energy estimates based on measurement-calibrated power models. Building on these models, you will explore how architectural choices—including network topology, link bandwidth, and parallelization strategies—affect performance and energy consumption. You will develop tools that help cluster designers evaluate promising configurations efficiently. You will also investigate how the models can guide runtime decisions, such as workload placement, prioritization, routing, or resource reservation. A focused prototype will demonstrate how model-informed decisions can improve the operation of an existing network. Experimental validation will be an integral part of your research. You will use measurements from AI infrastructure and conduct reproducible experiments on programmable networking testbeds. Technologies of interest include Ethernet-based AI networks, emerging Ultra Ethernet mechanisms, P4-programmable switches, and SmartNICs. Finally, you will evaluate the results from the testbeds on real AI infrastructure in collaboration with our partner SURF. Through this combination of theory, software development, and experimentation, you will contribute to more responsive and energy-efficient AI infrastructure. Il s’agira ensuite d’étendre le Set-Based Design afin de représenter des ensembles de solutions admissibles définis conjointement par des contraintes humaines et techniques. Are you interested in the communication networks behind modern AI systems? Would you like to combine mathematical modeling with experiments on programmable network hardware to make AI infrastructure faster and more energy-efficient? In this PhD project, you will develop models and orchestration methods for the networks that connect GPUs during large language model inference. Are you our next PhD candidate in high-performance AI networking?
 Your research challenge 
Large language models rely on powerful computing infrastructure to generate responses. When inference is distributed across […] requirements, complemented by energy estimates based on measurement-calibrated power models.
Building on these models, you will explore how architectural choices—including network topology, link bandwidth, and parallelization strategies—affect performance and energy consumption. You will develop tools that help cluster designers evaluate promising configurations efficiently.
You will also investigate how the models can guide runtime decisions, such as workload placement, prioritization, routing, or resource reservation. A focused prototype will demonstrate how model-informed decisions can improve the operation of an existing network.
Experimental validation will be an integral part of your research. You will use measurements from AI infrastructure and conduct reproducible experiments on programmable networking testbeds. Technologies of interest include Ethernet-based AI networks, emerging Ultra Ethernet mechanisms, P4-programmable switches, and SmartNICs. Finally, you will evaluate the results from the testbeds on real AI infrastructure in collaboration with our partner SURF .

Cochlea-Implantate sind hochwirksame Neuroprothesen, die Menschen mit hochgradigem Hörverlust ermöglichen, wieder Klänge wahrzunehmen und Sprache zu verstehen. Wie gut das Sprachverstehen nach der Implantation gelingt, ist individuell sehr unterschiedlich: Bei rund einem Viertel der Patientinnen und Patienten bleiben die Ergebnisse hinter den Erwartungen zurück, und verlässliche Prognosen zum individuellen Nutzen eines Cochlea-Implantats vor der Operation fehlen bislang. Hinweise deuten darauf hin, dass neben dem Hörorgan auch die Verarbeitung und Vernetzung im Gehirn eine wichtige Rolle spielen. Die SOUND Study untersucht, wie sich diese Erkenntnisse für individuellere Prognosen nutzen lassen.  Les détecteurs Micromegas sont des détecteurs gazeux utilisés en physique des particules et en physique nucléaire. La lecture optique consiste à observer, à l’aide d’une caméra, la lumière émise lors de l’amplification des électrons dans le détecteur. Cette technique offre de nouvelles possibilités pour visualiser l’ionisation et reconstruire les événements, notamment les trajectoires des particules. Cependant, les mélanges gazeux utilisés reposent souvent sur le CF4, un gaz à fort impact climatique, ce qui motive la recherche de solutions alternatives.

 Description du sujet
 Au CERN, l’expérience LHCb observe des protons entrer en collision des dizaines de millions de fois par seconde et doit décider, en temps réel, quelles collisions conserver. Aujourd’hui, cela repose sur des milliers de petits programmes écrits à la main, un par signal de physique, une approche qui ne passe plus à l’échelle. En parallèle, l’IA a été révolutionnée par les « modèles de fondation », ces grands modèles derrière des outils comme ChatGPT : on entraîne un seul grand modèle une fois sur d’énormes données, puis on le réutilise pour de nombreuses tâches. Cette thèse demande si l’on peut construire un tel modèle pour LHCb : une IA unique qui apprend à « lire » une collision entière et peut ensuite servir à de multiples études de physique. Tu construirais la première version de ce modèle, l’entraînerais directement sur de vraies données du CERN (et non seulement sur des simulations, ce qui fait son originalité), et montrerais qu’il se transfère d’une tâche à l’autre en nécessitant beaucoup moins d’étiquetage manuel. En chemin, tu apprendrais l’IA moderne de façon concrète (PyTorch, entraînement sur GPU) et l’analyse de données d’une expérience majeure. Aucune expertise préalable en IA n’est requise : …

The work is hosted at CEA/Irfu, alongside the HEPfoundry team building foundation models for physics, with partners at CERN/LHCb.

 Ce projet a pour but d’étudier la structure et les réactions des noyaux atomiques exotiques qui peuvent être faiblement liés, voire non liés. L’étude expérimentale de ces systèmes est possible à l’aide d’accélérateurs d’ions radioactifs. Ces noyaux présentent souvent des caractéristiques inhabituelles, telles que des structures en halo. Les modèles nucléaires traditionnels, efficaces pour les noyaux stables, ne parviennent pas à saisir les complexités de ces systèmes quantiques ouverts. Pour y remédier, le modèle en couches de Gamow (GSM) ainsi que son extension aux approches à canaux couplés (GSM-CC) ont été développés. Ils traitent les noyaux comme des systèmes ouverts capables d’échanger des particules et de l’énergie avec leur environnement. Cela permet une description unifiée de la structure et des réactions nucléaires, y compris les effets du continuum quantique, qui deviennent significatifs aux driplines.  Description du sujet
 Le calcul haute performance est aujourd’hui au cœur des activités de recherche. En particulier, la recherche fondamentale en physique nucléaire théorique repose sur des codes numériques performants pour réaliser des calculs ab initio des noyaux atomiques. Ces calculs permettent d’établir des prédictions systématiques, tant pour les études fondamentales des systèmes nucléaires que pour le soutien aux activités expérimentales. Des progrès considérables ont été réalisés ces dernières années sur cette thématique, ce qui a amené l’équipe du CEA à réaliser, en 2026, le calcul ab initio du noyau lourd U-238, une première dans ce domaine.
Malgré ces avancées, les calculs ab initio de structure nucléaire et, en particulier, les calculs de réactions impliquant des noyaux lourds demeurent extrêmement difficiles. Dans ce contexte, l’informatique quantique émerge comme un nouveau paradigme de calcul susceptible de bouleverser les approches actuelles et de contribuer à lever certains des verrous numériques existants.  Description du sujet
 La fragmentation, processus par lequel les quarks et les gluons se transforment en hadrons, ne peut pas être calculée à partir des premiers principes de la QCD et doit être extraite des données. Les fonctions de fragmentation dépendantes de l’impulsion transverse (TMDFF) sont particulièrement mal connues. L’observable la plus propre pour les contraindre est la distribution en impulsion transverse de paires pi+pi- quasiment dos à dos dans l’annihilation e+e-, mais aucune mesure de ce type n’existe. Das Projekt wird vom Forschungsteam «Auditory Pathway» am Hearing Research Laboratory des ARTORG Centers for Biomedical Engineering Research der Universität Bern in enger Zusammenarbeit mit der Universitätsklinik für […] s-, Nasen- und Ohrenkrankheiten am Inselspital durchgeführt. Cochlea-Implantate sind hochwirksame Neuroprothesen, die Menschen mit hochgradigem Hörverlust ermöglichen, wieder Klänge wahrzunehmen und Sprache zu verstehen. Wie gut das Sprachverstehen nach der Implantation gelingt, ist individuell sehr unterschiedlich: Bei rund einem Viertel der Patientinnen und Patienten bleiben die Ergebnisse hinter den Erwartungen zurück, und verlässliche Prognosen zum individuellen Nutzen eines Cochlea-Implantats vor der Operation fehlen bislang. Hinweise deuten darauf hin, dass neben dem Hörorgan auch die Verarbeitung und Vernetzung im Gehirn eine wichtige Rolle spielen. Die SOUND Study untersucht, wie sich diese Erkenntnisse für individuellere Prognosen nutzen lassen. Das erwartet Sie Im Rahmen der SOUND Study untersuchen Sie die zentralen Hörbahnen mithilfe neuester bildgebender Verfahren. Im Fokus stehen die funktionelle Nahinfrarotspektroskopie (fNIRS) und spezialisierte Magnetresonanztomografie-Sequenzen (MRT) Sie führen neurobildgebende, audiologische und klinische Daten zusammen und wenden statistische Verfahren sowie Machine Learning an, um Muster zu erkennen, die mit dem späteren Sprachverstehen zusammenhängen Ihre Ergebnisse diskutieren und interpretieren Sie gemeinsam mit Fachpersonen aus der Neuroradiologie sowie mit klinischen und technischen Expertinnen und Experten Das bringen …

 The Data-Driven Mechanics Laboratory invites applications for a fully funded PhD position at
the intersection of computational mechanics, multiphysics of geomaterials, and interpretable
machine learning. The project focuses on the discovery of governing equations and constitutive
relations for key multiphysics phenomena on the basis of rich micromechanical and
experimental data. It pushes the boundaries of modeling and understanding crucial processes
in geomaterials across scales, with application to geophysics, energy and sustainability.

● Excellent English communication skills (oral and written).

● Innovative interdisciplinary research at the Data-Driven Mechanics Lab.
● Exceptional research infrastructure and access to world-class computational resources.
● Competitive salary and employment conditions.

received. For inquiries please contact Prof. Kostas Karapiperis at the same email.

Mission
 At the Laboratory for Quantum Magnetism (LQM) we perform fundamental research in magnetism and correlated electron materials. Our core activities span from synthesis of novel materials over in-house experimental techniques in combination with low temperature, high pressures and high magnetic fields, neutron and X-ray scattering to theory and modeling. The LQM is part of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), a world-renowned research and education center, offering an ideal academic environment as well as an excellent connection to industry. 
 The available PhD position […] skills in English (spoken and written), and a willingness to learn and engage in challenging research. 
 We offer
 A challenging and exciting PhD project in experimental quantum magnetism, supervised by Dr. Ivica Živković and Prof. Henrik M. Rønnow. 
 Access to state-of-the-art experimental facilities for microwave spectroscopy of rare-earth quantum magnets. 
 Opportunities to perform measurements under low-temperature and high-magnetic-field conditions. 
 A stimulating and collaborative research environment within the Laboratory for Quantum Magnetism and the broader EPFL community. 
 Opportunities to present your research at international conferences and develop collaborations within the quantum magnetism community. 
 Informations
 Applications should include grade transcript, CV, motivation letter and three contact persons for references. For any further information, please contact Dr. Ivica Živković ( ivica.zivkovic@epfl.ch ). We encourage applications from candidates of all genders and diverse cultural and personal backgrounds . 
 The selected PhD student will need to enroll in the physics program of the EPFL doctoral school. After one year of successful probation, the initial contract will be extended up to a total of four years. Doctoral school information and employment conditions at EPFL are described at: 
 https://www.epfl.ch/education/phd/programs/edpy-physics

at-nl:363997.title: 2 PhD positions on Measuring the Future of Power Electronics
at-nl:363997.desc:
The challenge: 
Power electronics are central to renewable-energy systems, electric mobility, industrial electrification and modern power grids. New wide-bandgap semiconductor devices based on silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) can switch faster and reduce conversion losses, but their performance is increasingly difficult to measure with sufficient bandwidth, accuracy and traceability. When converter efficiencies exceed 99%, even very small measurement errors can obscure the losses that designers need to understand.
Within the EU Chips Joint Undertaking project Moore4Power, the […] requirements and characterization.

 You will collaborate intensively with academic and industrial partners across Europe, including regular project meetings, technical exchanges and work visits.
 You will have the freedom and responsibility to shape your research direction, develop advanced experimental skills and contribute to solutions with clear scientific and industrial relevance.
 Your profile for PhD 1: 
 An MSc degree in electrical engineering or a closely related field, with strong experimental academic results.
 A solid foundation in analogue electronics, RF or microwave engineering, wideband sensors, or high-frequency measurement techniques.
 Hands-on interest in designing, building and debugging new wideband current sensors.
 Experience with electromagnetic or circuit simulation, PCB design, vector network analysis or oscilloscope measurements is an advantage.
 The ability to combine theoretical modelling with careful laboratory work and quantitative data analysis.

boards-phd:linkedin:4483796912.desc: EDF R&D, avec ses 2000 chercheurs, a pour missions principales de contribuer à l'amélioration de la performance des unités opérationnelles du groupe EDF, d'identifier et de préparer les relais de croissance à moyen et long termes. EDF R&D met en œuvre une politique volontariste de partenariat en France et à l’international notamment dans les pays où le Groupe est présent. Vous souhaitez associer mécanique des matériaux, simulation numérique et intelligence artificielle pour répondre à des enjeux industriels ? > Rejoignez EDF Recherche et Développement dans le cadre d’une thèse CIFRE consacrée […] à la réduction de modèle par apprentissage profond pour les calculs en plasticité cristalline. La poursuite de l’exploitation des centrales nucléaires au-delà de 60 ans nécessite des outils avancés pour justifier la tenue mécanique des composants. Pour les matériaux métalliques, leur comportement dépend notamment de la microstructure, c’est-à-dire de l’organisation des grains qui les constituent. Les simulations en plasticité cristalline permettent de représenter ces grains et leurs interactions pour mieux comprendre les déformations et les mécanismes de rupture. Elles restent toutefois coûteuses en temps de calcul, ce qui limite l’étude de microstructures et de sollicitations variées. L’objectif de cette thèse est de développer des modèles réduits fondés sur l’apprentissage profond pour accélérer ces simulations, tout en conservant une précision adaptée aux grandeurs étudiées et en respectant les lois physiques. Vos principales missions seront les suivantes : Étudier les méthodes de réduction de modèle et d’apprentissage profond adaptées à la plasticité cristalline. Constituer et exploiter des jeux de données issus de simulations de référence, couvrant différentes microstructures, propriétés des matériaux et sollicitations mécaniques. boards-phd:linkedin:4417659196.desc: Titre de la thèse: Apprentissage par renforcement décentralisé, en vue d’une gestion intelligente des systèmes de stockage pour l’utilisation des ressources d’énergie renouvelable, associés au besoin de consommation : application à un quartier d’habitation. Une part croissante de la production d'énergie électrique est installée au sein des zones d’habitation notamment grâce aux panneaux solaires ou parfois aux éoliennes. Ainsi la gestion du réseau doit passer d’un système centralisé à une gestion localisée. À cela s’ajoute des nouveaux composants, comme l’introduction de la voiture […]  qui modifient les profils de consommation. Dans un objectif d’autonomie maximale, l’équilibre énergétique entre la production et la consommation électrique locale n’est réalisable qu’en utilisant des moyens de stockage aussi bien électrique que thermique. L’objectif de cette thèse est de rechercher des algorithmes d’apprentissage par renforcement pour la gestion d’une grille électrique (production, consommation, stockage) ayant pour critère un degré d’autonomie maximal. La solution doit être adaptable et adaptative pour prendre en compte les différents profils de comportements. La modélisation de la grille énergétique sous toutes ses facettes est un élément primordial pour cet objectif. Vous serez également chargé de rédiger des rapports annuels détaillés ainsi que des articles destinés à des conférences et des journaux spécialisés.  ETH Zurich is one of the leading universities worldwide and renowned for its excellence in education, fundamental and applied research, and technology transfer. At the Institute for Biomedical Engineering, one research focus is on nuclear magnetic resonance. The team of Prof. Klaas Prüssmann drives innovation in magnetic resonance from physical and mathematical principles all […] the way to novel imaging, sensing, and tracking technology. In close collaboration with academic and industrial partners, we pursue applications in the biomedical realm, process engineering, and materials science. One recent focus of interest is on the use of magnetic resonance for particle tracking in granular systems. We are looking for a Physicist or Engineer to join us on this frontier as a Doctoral Student.
 Project background
 Granular systems are ubiquitous in nature and of fundamental importance to industry, from food and pharma to material conversion. However, despite their widespread occurence and use, many important phenomena such as the transition between flowing and solid states, mixing, segregation, or surface instabilities, are poorly understood. Magnetic resonance has proven a powerful means of studying granular physics, permitting both dynamic imaging and, newly, the tracking of particle swarms. The focus is now on further expanding the tracking strategies and, in the applied realm, on exploring the role of the shape of particles and how granular dynamics change when particles are soft and deform upon stress.

industrial:bosch:744000158262769.desc:
Wir forschen an hochmodernen Deep Generative Models, die dazu dienen, reale Bosch-Systeme dateneffizient zu machen. Wir suchen eine:n Doktorandin bzw. Doktoranden, der sich für die Erforschung kreativer Anwendungen generativer Modelle (z.B. Stable Diffusion) als kontrollierbare Datensatzdarstellung für Training sowie Validierung von Netzwerken für nachgelagerte Aufgaben interessiert.
 Nicht alle Datenpunkte in einem Datensatz sind gleichermaßen wichtig für die Leistung eines neuronalen Netzwerks. Mit fortschreitendem Training ist der Verlust einiger Datenpunkte möglicherweise nicht mehr […] ekräftig, da das Netzwerk bereits alles daraus gelernt hat, was es kann. Daher kann es von Vorteil sein, das Netzwerktraining zu beobachten, um die richtigen Daten zur richtigen Zeit bereitzustellen. Allerdings ist die Auswahl von Daten aus einem festen Datensatz problematisch, wenn kein Bild mit der genauen Mischung von Attributen vorhanden ist. Ziel dieses Doktorandenprojekts ist die Entwicklung neuer Lernalgorithmen zur Generierung relevanter Daten „on Demand“ als Reaktion auf den Bedarf des Netzwerks. Dazu gehört unter anderem die Verbesserung der Trainingseffizienz durch die Synthese von Daten besserer Relevanz sowie durch gezielte Erstellung von Beispielen sicherzustellen, dass die gewünschte Invarianz erzielt wird.
 Als Teil unseres Teams entwickeln Sie neuartige Ansätze zur Anpassung von Deep Generative Models (z.B. Diffusion Models, GANs, VAEs) als Datenquellen, um nachgelagerte Modelle besser zu trainieren und zu validieren.
 Darüber hinaus nutzen Sie die Steuerbarkeit und das Wissen generativer Basismodelle, um Datensätze nicht mehr nur als eine lose Sammlung von Bildern zu betrachten.
 Sie diskutieren sowie entwickeln neue Ideen mit den Expertinnen bzw. Experten für Deep Learning und Computer Vision im Bosch Center for AI.
 Darüber hinaus haben Sie die Möglichkeit, Ihre Ergebnisse in hochrangigen Fachzeitschriften und Konferenzen zu veröffentlichen.

Nicht alle Datenpunkte in einem Datensatz sind gleichermaßen wichtig für die Leistung eines neuronalen Netzwerks. Ziel dieses Doktorandenprojekts ist die Entwicklung neuer Lernalgorithmen zur Generierung relevanter Daten „on Demand“ als Reaktion auf den Bedarf des Netzwerks. Dazu gehört unter anderem die Verbesserung der Trainingseffizienz durch die Synthese von Daten besserer Relevanz sowie durch gezielte Erstellung von Beispielen sicherzustellen, dass die gewünschte Invarianz erzielt wird. Domaine d'activité PhD position on a project funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF), entitled Breaking Barriers: How Gender Stereotypes in French and Swiss Schoolbooks Affect Young Learners’ Processing difficulties, Motivation and Interest . School textbooks not only influence learning outcomes, but also shape how children perceive girls and boys, how they envision themselves within school subjects, and how they imagine their future careers. Our project examines how women, men, girls, and boys are represented in primary school textbooks in Switzerland (both French-speaking and German-speaking regions) and in France, through both images and language. We seek to understand whether these representations reinforce or challenge gender stereotypes, and how they affect pupils’ motivation, interest, and learning. The ultimate goal is to contribute to the development of more inclusive educational resources that can support the potential and aspirations of all children. The project is funded for a period of four years. Knowledge of French is an asset. Mission 
 We are offering a full-time (100%) PhD position at ENAC at EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland, within the Plant Ecology Research Laboratory (PERL): https://www.epfl.ch/labs/perl/ 
The PhD project will investigate how forest canopy temperature and spectral properties reflect tree physiological responses to increasing atmospheric drought and soil water limitation. The overarching objective is to understand how forests regulate canopy temperature and water use under drought and to use thermal and spectral signals to map forest vulnerability from individual trees to large spatial scales.

The BRIDGE-AI doctoral network is employing 15 ambitious doctoral candidates at various locations in Europe (Finland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and Austria). We are currently inviting applications for the last 3 open PhD positions, located in Germany and Finland (see below). The aim of the BRIDGE-AI network is to develop new and trustworthy AI methods for longitudinal neuroimage analysis, helping clinical experts assess temporal changes in patients with chronic brain disorders. More information about the project is available from the BRIDGE-AI website .
DC1: Deep learning for cortical surface-based analyses (Bonn, Germany)
Employer: German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE)
Main supervisor: Prof. Dr. Martin Reuter

Are you passionate about advancing neuroscience and clinical applications through cutting-edge AI technology? Do you want to contribute to tools that can transform how we understand brain function, study neurological diseases, and evaluate large-scale population studies? Join us to develop innovative AI methods for cortical surface modeling – an essential foundation for modern neuroimaging research.

Why This Matters: The cerebral cortex, with its intricate folds and complex structure, holds key insights into brain health and disease. Accurate modeling and analysis of the cortical surface enable breakthroughs in understanding brain development, detecting abnormalities, and tracking disease progression. Your work will help build powerful AI tools that can improve diagnosis, guide treatment strategies, and push the boundaries of neuroscience research.
In this PhD project, you will:
Develop advanced AI methods to segment brain cortical atlases based on surface data, moving beyond traditional approaches.
Create algorithms to detect anomalies on the cortical surface, such as Focal Cortical Dysplasia (FCD), aiding early diagnosis of neurological conditions.
Innovate deep learning solutions for longitudinal surface extraction, tracking brain changes over time with unprecedented accuracy.
Implement state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for cross-subject and cross-time surface registration.
Thoroughly validate your methods to ensure broad applicability in neuroimaging workflows.

DC9: Interpretable prediction of gestational age from fetal brain MRI across institutions (Espoo, Finland)
PhD enrollment: Aalto University , Espoo, Finland
Main supervisor: prof. Koen Van Leemput

PhD project description: The assessment of whether a fetus is at the expected development stage is currently performed in a rather primitive fashion in the clinic: clinicians manually perform 2D measurements from fetal brain MRI scans, and compare those to normative growth curves to see whether development is delayed. In this PhD project, you will significantly advance this state of affairs by developing new probabilistic generative models of the developing neuroanatomy across gestational ages, and use those models to accurately estimate the gestational age from fetal MRI scans.

This is a highly relevant but also very ambitious project: In order to be fully clinically useful, the methods and tools that you will develop should work “out-of-the-box” on data that is acquired with different scanners, image resolutions, reconstruction algorithms and acquisition protocols. Furthermore, your models should encode the cause-effect relationship between gestational age and the acquired MRI scans, so that the obtained predictions are inherently interpretable for clinicians (for instance, by generating counterfactuals simulating a particular fetus’s neuroanatomy at different gestational ages). Once you are confident in the performance of your methods and tools, you should also apply them to large clinical datasets of both normal and abnormal brain development.

Your profile: This position requires strong skills in both math (e.g., linear algebra, Bayesian statistics) and coding (e.g., Python/NumPy, C++). Prior experience with medical imaging is not required.

DC14: Longitudinal progression markers derived from WM and GM alterations in different epilepsy phenotypes (Espoo, Finland)
PhD enrollment: Aalto University , Espoo, Finland
Main supervisors: prof. Koen Van Leemput & Dr. Richard McKinley (Bern, Switzerland)

Clinical Problem : Among patients who present with a first seizure, approximately 45% will have a further seizure within the next five years. Identifying which patients are likely to have recurrent seizures is therefore vitally important, since early treatment can dramatically improve the lives of patients with epilepsy and spare them from further neurological deficits brought on by repeated seizures.

Structural brain lesions are the most common cause of epileptic seizures, but the mere presence of a lesion is not predictive of epilepsy: the size and location of the lesion, and its proximity to the grey matter, are critical factors. Similarly, while loss of grey matter is seen in all epilepsy patients over time, specific patterns of grey-matter atrophy can be associated to different epilepsy subtypes. Identifying these patterns in a timely manner has the potential to drive patient treatment.

Your solution : In this PhD project you will develop methods to link patterns of grey- and white-matter alterations to epilepsy subtypes and to distinguish epilepsy patients from those with epilepsy mimics. You will benchmark and extend existing segmentation methods for quantifying white matter lesions and grey matter atrophy, and establish baselines for linking alterations and disease, such as lesion-symptom mapping and structural covariance networks. You will then explore how generative modeling can be harnessed to translate patterns of brain alteration into low-dimensional latent codes which capture the essence of a patient’s deviation from normal brain appearance, and harness these codes to better estimate a patient’s risk of receiving a definitive epilepsy diagnosis. The methods developed will be based on data from, and have direct application in, ongoing studies at the University Hospital Bern and across Switzerland, which aim to identify patients at high risk of developing epilepsy after a first seizure, and to study the effects of epilepsy over time on the structure, function and metabolism of the brain.

This Doctoral Network will provide its Doctoral Candidates with a rigorous training in solving complex problems characterised by many degrees of freedom and intrinsic noise, all of which arise in the context of biological systems and are key to functions as movement, growth and regulation. Each Doctoral Candidate will pursue research within one of the PhD Research Projects described below, utilising techniques from statistical and condensed matter physics to discover how collective phenomena emerge in biological systems from interactions between their component parts.

A distinctive feature of this Doctoral Network is that a novel combination of modelling and analysis techniques, which traditionally have each been applied in a specific problem domain, lies at the heart of each PhD research project. For this reason, Doctoral Candidates will each have two supervisors, one at the primary host institution (indicated in the panels below), and another at a second institution in the network, with a period of research at the second institution, fully funded by the programme, designed into the research projects. Some projects additionally feature secondments with our non-academic partners.

Full details of project goals, methodologies, hosting and secondment arrangements are provided within each description below. Recruitment is now completed with offers made to the successful candidates. All PhD projects are to begin on September 1st 2026 or as soon as possible thereafter.
Bayesian inference of active Brownian motion

For the study of motile cells and other self-propelled particles it is often key to extract quantitative features from trajectories of these particles, both to quantify experimental trajectories and to parametrise theoretical models.
Beyond the extensile/contractile dichotomy in active nematics
Active nematics is one of the most studied situations in active matter physics, both in theory and experiments.
The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Bottom-up modelling of dense bacterial suspensions
Dense active suspensions, such as those formed by swarming bacteria, constitute a type of active matter that is particularly hard to model.
Collective tug-of-war dynamics: from molecular motors to ant groups
The emergence of directed transport as a collective behaviour of many microscopic constituents is a ubiquitous problem in the statistical physics of active particles.
The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Control theory for topological active matter
Experimental techniques have demonstrated the ability to alter the collective dynamics of active systems with various types of external perturbations.
Defect dynamics in pulsating active matter

Some collective states in active matter exhibit topological properties through the formation of vortices and defects. In some living systems, defects have been shown to have important biological functions.
Dense active matter and the cage escape dynamics of active particles
Passive particles form amorphous solids or glasses at high densities. The same is true of active particles that model living matter such as confluent tissues.

The dynamics of the sperm flagellum has been recently studied with particular attention to its fluctuations. It has been found that the precision of the flagellar beating is close to that of an individual dynein motor powering its motion, which in turn is close to the bound dictated by the thermodynamic uncertainty relation.
NANOTEC-CNR/The Sapienza University of Rome, Italy

Collective tissue behaviour is inherently a multiscale phenomenon that is governed by complex biochemical and mechanical processes occurring simultaneously at the molecular, cellular, and tissue scales.
Exploring active field theories to unravel solidification of protein condensates

The spatial organisation of proteins into dense condensates, widely attributed to nonequilibrium phase separation, offers a route to recruit or sequester proteins involved in functions at the cellular level.
Growth of cells in viscoelastic medium

Typically, the complex environments in which living systems reside are viscoelastic fluids. For example, the extracellular matrix comprises cross-linked, semiflexible polymeric filaments that respond sensitively to even small stresses generated by cells.
Institute of Physical Chemistry Polish Academy of Sciences, Poland

Owing to their active nature, interactions between migrating cells can be non-reciprocal. However, the extent to which cells control their collective behaviour through non-reciprocal interactions remains unclear.
Active field theories are widely used to study collective effects in driven systems at all levels of organisation, allowing instabilities to pattern formation to be identified.
The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom

While active matter theory has successfully advanced our understanding of the collective dynamics resulting from individual sources of activity, multiple active processes usually act in concert in real biological systems.
Max-Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization/University of Göttingen, Germany
Statistical mechanics of motility and growth within extracellular matrices

Collective cellular activity and self-organisation phenomena arising from non-equilibrium activity are ubiquitous in tissues and cellular aggregates. However, the relationship between individual properties and biological patterns remains unexplored.

Decoding and designing biomolecular systems with hybrid DNA:RNA:protein nanotechnology

Our increasing knowledge of the fundamental mechanisms of life and the confluence of techniques are the basis for the development of novel life-inspired technologies. In recent years, notably in the development of COVID-19 vaccines, we have witnessed the pivotal role played by RNA in nanomedical advancements. At the same time, DNA nanotechnology has already proven to yield some of the most complex, yet well controlled, artificial biomolecular structures.

Taking these different ingredients together, our abilities of building bottom-up functional machines and biomolecular systems involving DNA, RNA and proteins are currently emerging quicker than ever before, with new prospects for drug design and delivery, biosensors, as well as complex biomolecular robots and materials.

To unlock the full potential for complex biosensing devices that modularly emulate life-like functions and interact in complex biomolecular environments, BioHYBRITE brings together a unique team of world leading academics in the forefront of relevant bottom-up hybrid nanotechnologies, through the EU Horizon Europe MSCA DN funding scheme (Grant Agreement Nr. 101227379).

Which positions are open, and when should I apply? Check the vacancy listings and individual doctoral project pages for open positions. Each university advertisement specifies its own application window, requirements and deadline.

How do I submit an application? Read the doctoral project page, then follow its link to the recruiting university’s official advertisement. Submit your application through the procedure specified there. Vacancies will also be advertised on EURAXESS. The EMANAIRE website provides information and links; it does not receive applications.

Can I apply to more than one project? Yes. You may apply to up to four EMANAIRE doctoral projects. Submit a separate application for each position. In each motivation or cover letter, briefly identify your other EMANAIRE applications, including any you intend to submit, using the project numbers or titles. Tailor each application to the project concerned.

What academic background do I need? We welcome applicants interested in the human and organisational implications of AI. Relevant backgrounds may include management, organisation studies, psychology, sociology, communication and information systems. Each project has its own academic, methodological and language requirements, and you must meet the host university’s doctoral admission requirements.

Can I apply if I am still completing my master’s degree? This depends on the university. Check its advertisement for when your qualifying degree must be completed and what evidence you should provide. Contact the recruiting university if you are unsure whether your expected graduation date meets its requirements.

Can applicants of any nationality apply? Yes. MSCA Doctoral Network positions are open to applicants of any nationality. You must also satisfy the mobility rule, doctoral-status condition and the recruiting university’s admission and employment requirements. Visa or residence-permit arrangements depend on your circumstances and the host country.

What is the MSCA mobility rule? In general, you must not have lived or carried out your main activity, such as work or study, in the recruiting country for more than 12 months in the 36 months immediately before recruitment. This is assessed separately for each recruiting country. The university will check your circumstances and any applicable exceptions; consult its advertisement for the full conditions.

Can I apply if I already have a doctorate? You must not hold a doctoral degree when recruited. Researchers who have successfully defended a doctoral thesis are also ineligible, even if the degree has not yet been formally awarded.

Which documents should I prepare? Follow the individual university advertisement. Requirements may include a CV, motivation letter, degree certificates and transcripts, references, a research proposal and evidence of MSCA eligibility. Proposal lengths and document formats differ between hosts. Use the official instructions for each application rather than one standard document package.

Are the positions funded, and how long do they last? The doctoral positions are supported through EMANAIRE’s MSCA funding. Salary, allowances, contract duration and any additional institutional funding are specified by each recruiting university. Check each advertisement for its own employment terms.

Where will I be based, and will I travel? You will be based at the host university listed for your project and join shared network activities. Planned secondments and academic visits provide experience in other research and professional settings. The arrangements for your position, including travel and timing, will be explained by the host university.
When would the doctorate start? Start dates may differ between universities. Follow the intended start date and any flexibility stated in each official university advertisement.

Who can answer questions or help with application adjustments? Use the contact named in the relevant university advertisement for project questions, eligibility checks or reasonable adjustments to the application and selection process. For general questions about the network, contact the EMANAIRE coordinator.

You will develop your project at a host university while joining an international community of doctoral researchers and supervisors. Shared schools, methods workshops and research seminars will support your work, with planned secondments connecting your research to organisations outside academia. Employment terms and application requirements are set out in each official advertisement.
​ Project title: Machine learning-guided multiparametric optimisation of cytochrome P450 monooxygenase

The aim of this project is to simultaneously improve the activity and stability of cytochrome P450 BM3, minimizing trade-off effects and enabling a smoother transition to larger-scale application. To enable this, Lisa will develop a workflow applying high-throughput screening to generate experimental data on the enzyme's sequence and functional properties, which will be used to iteratively train a predictive machine learning model.
Background fields: s tructural biology, molecular biology

Project title: Multiparametric engineering of alkene dioxygenase

Sebastián's project is focused on the characterization and improvement of non-heme iron dependent Alkene Dioxigenases, in a multiparametric approach. He will use both rational design and random mutagenesis to accomplish his goals of improving the fitness of our collection of alkene dioxigenases.

Project title: Engineering conformational dynamics and mechanism in oxygenases

The project focuses on the computationally guided design of oxygenases through the engineering of enzyme conformational dynamics and catalytic mechanism. The project aims to understand how changes in protein sequence, including mutations at residues distant from the active site can reshape the conformational ensamble of oxygenases and thereby improve activity and selectivity. In particular, Shortest Path Map (SPM) analyses are used to investigate communication networks within the enzyme and identify pathways connecting distal residues to the active site.
Background fields: b ioinformatics, machine-learning, drug discovery workflows, cheminformatics

Project title: Kinetic stability data collection for predictive bioprocess modelling of CYP enzymes

The main objectives of this project are to understand how dissolved oxygen affects enzyme stability in a bioprocess-realistic environment, as well as to develop a hybrid model to predict enzyme stability across different reactors and conditions. The project will involve a scale-down approach, with a focus on gathering relevant stability data for P450. The collected data will then be used for the development of a hybrid model utilizing active learning and machine learning. The initial work will focus on isolated enzymes, with the ambition of expanding the model to whole-cell systems.
Background fields: m olecular biotechnology, fermentation, biocatalysis
Project title : Process intensification of cytochrome P450 reactions in batch and continuous reactors

This project focuses on intensifying cytochrome P450-catalysed reactions in batch and continuous-flow reactors. Controlled bioreactor experiments and reaction engineering will be used to investigate how substrate supply, and the delivery of oxygen or hydrogen peroxide influence reaction efficiency and productivity. In collaboration with WP1, engineered P450 variants will be evaluated under process-relevant conditions, while the resulting kinetic and process data will contribute to modelling and machine-learning activities in WP3. Selected reactions will also be investigated in pressurized continuous-flow systems to improve oxygen availability. By identifying key process bottlenecks and developing scale-up criteria, the project aims to connect enzyme engineering with robust and scalable biocatalytic production.
Background fields : biotechnology, biochemistry, biocatalysis, bioprocess engineering, continuous-flow biocatalysis
Project title: Process development and optimization of dioxygenase catalysed biotransformation

The project is process development and optimisation of dioxygenase-catalysed biotransformation based on the conversion of isoeugenol to vanillin, focusing on biocatalyst operational stability under bioreactor conditions. The research will combine experimental biocatalyst development, kinetic characterization, mathematical modelling, and in silico process intensification and validation.
Background fields: e nzyme bioprocess, reaction engineering, process intensification, machine learning
Project title: Continuous flow oxyfunctionalisations of allylic substrates catalysed by UPOs

The aim of this project is to develop efficient and reusable unspecific peroxygenase (UPO) biocatalysts for selective oxyfunctionalization. Nektaria will combine protein engineering and process engineering to improve UPO activity, selectivity, stability, and reusability for allylic oxyfunctionalization. Diverse UPOs and allylic substrates will be screened to identify promising enzyme–substrate combinations, while enzyme immobilization, continuous-flow operation, and controlled H₂O₂ supply will be explored to enhance overall catalytic and process performance, enabling more efficient and sustainable oxyfunctionalization chemistry.
Background fields: biotechnology, biochemistry, biocatalysis, protein engineering, and bioprocess engineering
Project title: Machine learning-based tools for multiparametric enzyme optimisation

Daniela's project focuses on developing machine learning-based tools for multiparametric enzyme optimisation. Building on protein mutational datasets generated in-house for a range of enzymes, as well as public protein databases, she will explore and compare state-of-the-art data representation techniques to build next-generation data-driven models for engineering properties such as enzyme activity, selectivity, stability and solubility.
Background fields: computational chemistry, bioinformatics, molecular dynamics
Project title: Development of machine learned coarse grained force fields for computational enzyme design

Filippo works on machine-learned force-fields for enzyme systems — neural network models that learn from reference data the potential energy surface governing how these proteins move. He is particularly interested in coarse-grained models, which enable the simulation of long-timescale dynamics. He is also interested in explainability and interpretability methods, which make machine-learning models transparent rather than black boxes: understanding what the network has learned about the underlying physics and why it produces a given prediction, both to trust the simulations and to extract mechanistic insight into how enzymes work.
Project title: Development of ML-based tools for analysis and engineering protein dynamics

Tillman’s project focuses on developing machine-learning tools to analyse and engineer protein dynamics. These movements and conformational changes play a central role in how enzymes function. The project aims to move beyond static protein structures by developing efficient methods to predict, understand, and deliberately modify dynamic behaviour. He will also develop AI-assisted workflows that support the progression from researching a target protein and computationally screening designs to prioritizing candidates for experimental validation. The broader goal is to establish protein dynamics as a practical component of protein design, enabling useful enzyme variants to be identified with fewer experiments and less computation.
Background fields: machine learning, bioinformatics, scientific software engineering, agentic workflows
Project title: EVB- and AI-guided Engineering of Unspecific Peroxygenases (UPOs) for Selective Benzylic Hydroxylation

Biya's project combines computational methods and machine learning to engineer unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) for selective benzylic C–H hydroxylation, a reaction that competes with off-target epoxidation and overoxidation. Towards this, she will build calibrated EVB/QM/MM models of the enzyme's reaction mechanism to understand how its structure governs this selectivity, and use these insights to propose targeted mutations. The collected simulation data will then be used to develop an uncertainty-aware active learning model that prioritises the enzyme variants most worth testing, rather than screening them all. The project also extends into process engineering, modelling how the enzyme performs under real operating conditions to support its future use at an industrial scale. This combination of mechanistic simulation and data-driven prediction is intended to identify UPO variants and operating conditions that improve selectivity and productivity, with fewer experiments than conventional screening would require.
Background fields: theoretical and computational chemistry, molecular dynamics simulation
Project title: Hybrid models for data-driven bioprocess optimization

Athina's project focuses on developing novel machine learning methods for the design and optimization of bioprocesses in biocatalysis. The objective is to develop an algorithmic toolbox for bioprocess optimization, scale-down process development, control and transfer learning across different processes. The optimization aims to maximize process outcome and minimize experimental resources. Regarding scale-up and scale-down, variable mismatches arise between scales, leading to different effects on the process. For control, the goal is to achieve real-time control under uncertainty, accounting for the nonlinear and dynamic nature of the system. The model will be applied to UPO, CYP and DO production processes, using hybrid models as the modeling method.
Background fields: bioprocess engineering, hybrid modeling, machine learning

HEAL4WARD opens call for 11 fully funded PhD positions in advanced wound care research

The HEAL4WARD project has officially launched its open call for applications to recruit 11 Doctoral Candidates (DCs) within its Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Network. The programme offers fully funded PhD positions for early-stage researchers interested in advancing next-generation solutions for wound infection diagnosis and treatment.

HEAL4WARD’s research programme combines expertise across nanomaterials, antimicrobial strategies, 3D printing, advanced sensing technologies and artificial intelligence to enable more precise and personalised infection management. DCs will contribute to interdisciplinary projects addressing challenges such as biofilm-related infections, real-time diagnostics and targeted antimicrobial therapies.
A unique MSCA doctoral training experience

HEAL4WARD provides a comprehensive doctoral training programme aligned with the MSCA Doctoral Network model, combining scientific excellence with structured skills development. Selected candidates will benefit from:
Full-time employment contracts with competitive salaries and social benefits in line with MSCA regulations
Joint supervision by leading academic, clinical and industrial partners
Access to high-quality research infrastructures and interdisciplinary expertise

A key feature of the programme is its strong emphasis on mobility and international exposure. Throughout the programme, each DC will undertake secondments with other organisations within the HEAL4WARD consortium, including academic institutions, clinical environments and industrial partners. These secondments are designed to extend learning beyond the host institution, allowing candidates to gain practical experience in different sectors, strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration and better understand the translation of research into real-world healthcare solutions. DCs will be hosted across multiple European countries, including institutions in Ireland, Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and other partner locations, reflecting the network’s broad geographic coverage.

In addition to their individual research projects, DCs will participate in a comprehensive network-wide training programme designed to complement their scientific development. This includes thematic training schools and specialised workshops, as well as dedicated courses on transferable skills such as scientific communication, entrepreneurship, intellectual property management and research ethics. The programme also facilitates active engagement with stakeholders across academia, healthcare systems and industry, ensuring that candidates develop a well-rounded skill set and are equipped for diverse career pathways both within and beyond academia.

GENOME: GENerative and connected intelligence for 6G Open ManagemEnt

AI and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to handle complex tasks across many fields. In network management, they offer powerful tools to automate operations, improve efficiency, and optimise performance. Supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions programme, the GENOME project aims to design, develop, and test LLM-based solutions for the autonomous management of different network domains. GENOME sets the following ambitious research objectives (ROs):
RO-A. Design GenAI/scalable mixture of experts (MoE)-based models for network management, especially at edge.
RO-B. Design methods for automatic configuration generation of softwarized edge and RAN network segments and task planning.
RO-C. Develop new multi-agent communication-based protocols in the future-proof 6G O-RAN .

RO-D. Design transparent and resilient AI functions by developing AI act-aligned in-hoc XAI methods for LLMs/SLMs in 6G O-RAN as well as building context for AI security systems via LLMs and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) .

MEDIculous REMeDy offers 15 fully funded doctoral positions through the European Union's Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Networks program. Doctoral candidates are expected to start their positions between June and October 2027, depending on the recruiting institution and local procedures.

The project coordination team verifies that applicants fulfil the MSCA eligibility criteria and the admission requirements of the respective host institution.

DC9 Modelling of the dynamic response for offshore wind farms - This position is now filled

The combination of a long coastline, shallow water, and offshore wind makes the UK one of the best locations in the world for wind power. As of 2023, the UK has over 11,000 wind turbines generating 30 GW of power, which accounts for almost 30% of the UK electricity supply. The UK Government has committed to increase the offshore capacity to 50 GW by 2030. Despite these significant benefits and enthusiasm for wind power, there are some serious challenges, which have become apparently in the last two decades 1) Clusters of turbines can produce powerful standing waves, in both air and seawater, severely affecting wildlife and radar and sonar operations. 2) Wind turbines are gyroscopic systems that possess highly complex chiral vibrational modes. Candidates must hold a Master’s degree (or equivalent) in a relevant discipline and demonstrate strong motivation and scientific potential. Each DC will sign a 3-year contract with the host institution, receive a competitive MSCA salary (including mobility and family allowances), and participate in secondments at partner organisations. Applications will be advertised globally through EURAXESS and other channels, and selection will involve a fair, inclusive process aligned with Horizon Europe standards.
Explore the positions below to learn more about each opportunity:
DC1: Designing necroptosis/NAFLD modulators with one-shot learning (Mentor: Tiago Rodrigues, University of Lisbon, Portugal)
Host: FARM-ID, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Lisbon Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes
This PhD project will explore few-shot learning and anomaly detection in medicinal chemistry to design novel modulators targeting necroptosis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

Key objectives: • Expand the ligand space of RIPK3 and prioritise molecules for synthesis using advanced ML strategies • Apply transfer learning (LSTMs) and Siamese neural networks for bioactivity prediction • Develop generative models and anomaly detection approaches for de novo molecule design • Evaluate up to 10 candidate molecules through synthesis and biological validation
The candidate will also contribute to building curated datasets and sustainable drug design workflows.
Planned secondments: • 3 months at TUE for deep learning expertise • 3 months at IBM for LLMs in drug design • 6 months at AC for synthesis of small molecules
DC2: Agentic AI for drug discovery (Mentor: Samuel Genheden, AstraZeneca, Sweden)
Host: AZ Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project will focus on introducing novel reaction types into retrosynthesis planning tools using machine learning models trained on chemoinformatics rules and ab initio data. The goal is to enhance predictive capabilities for synthetic pathways by combining computational chemistry and AI-driven approaches.

Key objectives: • Develop automatic pipelines for ab initio calculations of novel reaction types • Extract descriptors from chemical reactions to train ML models for retrosynthesis • Build prediction models (retro, forward, and condition) to assess feasibility and optimise reaction conditions • Integrate novel reaction types into multi-step retrosynthesis algorithms and evaluate their impact
The candidate will also contribute to creating open-source tools for deriving ML models from ab initio data and validating selected reaction types experimentally.

Planned secondments: • 5 months at EPFL to advance deep learning methods for synthetic pathway prediction • 3 months at ARQ to develop QM/ML approaches • 4 months at BGU to strengthen skills in synthetic chemistry
📌 Enrolment: Doctoral degree at EPFL 🔗 Learn more about the application HER E!
DC3: Tuning ADC payload release with active learning (Mentor: Gonçalo Bernardes, University of Cambridge, UK)
Host: UCAM Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project aims to optimise the release of payloads in antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) by tuning linker structures and payload properties using active learning approaches. The focus will be on controlling payload release through modulation of pKa values and chemical derivatisation strategies, improving therapeutic precision in cancer treatment.

Key objectives: • Develop an active learning loop to predict and optimise payload release from ADCs • Establish correlations between linker structure, payload pKa, and release rates in cells • Implement ML models to identify optimal substitution patterns for controlled release • Validate predictions through synthesis and experimental testing in vitro and in vivo
The candidate will also contribute to applying these strategies in real-world scenarios, including bioconjugation for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) therapy.

Planned secondments: • 6 months at FARM-ID to implement ML models and synthesis workflows • 3 months at ARQ and AZ for deep learning and bioconjugation development • GIMM and Hospital Santa Maria will provide biological materials for validation
DC4: Few-shot deep learning to discover novel PPARγ partial agonists (Mentor: Francesca Grisoni, Technical University Eindhoven, The Netherlands)
Host: TUE Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project will explore causal deep learning as an innovative approach to drug discovery, focusing on identifying novel PPARγ partial agonists. By leveraging small datasets and reusable causal relations, the project aims to overcome limitations of current algorithms and enable robust, generalisable models for low-data scenarios.

Key objectives: • Investigate how causality can be incorporated into molecular machine learning • Develop causal deep learning models for structure–activity prediction and ligand-protein interactions • Apply few-shot learning to discover new PPARγ partial agonists using commercially available libraries • Validate causal inference and refine models through iterative experimental cycles
The candidate will also contribute to designing easy-to-use ML tools for medicinal chemistry and generating insights for hit-to-lead optimisation.
Planned secondments: • 4 months at IBM to expand expertise in ML algorithms • 8 months combined at BRFAA and CSIC to gain hands-on experience in medicinal chemistry
📌 Enrolment: Doctoral degree at TUE 🔗 Learn more about the application HER E!
DC5: ML for the optimization of generality of synthetic methods (Mentor: Frank Glorius, University of Münster, Germany)

This PhD project will develop data science and machine learning workflows to improve the generality of modern synthetic methods. The goal is to identify structural motifs and reaction conditions that enable broad applicability across diverse substrates and functional groups, using advanced screening and optimisation strategies.
• Detect underrepresented structural patterns accessible by modern synthetic methods
• Assess generality of key reactions using ML-driven screening and Bayesian optimisation
• Apply iterative global optimisation algorithms to refine reaction conditions efficiently
• Validate optimised reactions experimentally and integrate findings into retrosynthesis tools
The candidate will also contribute to creating predictive models for reaction generality and applying them to drug-like compound synthesis.
• 4 months at FARM-ID to extend expertise in ML-based reaction optimisation
• 4 months at AZ to test optimisation approaches in real-world applications
• 4 months at AC to integrate ML tools into SDL technologies
DC6: Designing accurate molecular features for the small data regime (Mentor: Anat Milo, Ben Gurion University, Israel)

This PhD project combines computational, statistical, and synthetic approaches to design highly accurate molecular descriptors tailored for small data scenarios. The aim is to improve predictive modelling in catalysis and synthetic chemistry by creating descriptors that capture mechanistic details and functional group compatibility.
• Develop and benchmark new molecular descriptors for reaction component encoding
• Design and prepare novel catalyst structures based on these descriptors
• Apply descriptors to challenging organocatalytic reactions, such as enantioselective intermolecular Stetter reactions
• Uncover mechanistic insights and new selective transformations through data-driven analysis
The candidate will also contribute to integrating these descriptors into ML workflows for sustainable drug design.
• 4 months at EPFL to develop ML methods and benchmark descriptors
• 4 months at AZ to apply descriptors in predictive modelling
• 4 months at AC to integrate ML technologies into SDL frameworks
DC7: Design of novel c-Myc inhibitors using ML and physics-based approaches (Mentor: Zoe Cournia, BRFAA, Greece)

This PhD project focuses on discovering small-molecule inhibitors that disrupt c-Myc–Max dimerization, a key target in cancer therapy. The approach combines machine learning and physics-based simulations to efficiently screen large compound libraries and predict binding affinities, reducing computational costs and improving hit identification.
• Train N-shot neural networks to identify putative inhibitors from large compound databases
• Apply virtual screening and empirical scoring functions to prioritise candidates
• Perform MD simulations on c-Myc peptide structures to assess stability and binding
• Validate top-ranked compounds through biophysical and cell-based assays
The candidate will also contribute to developing robust ML models for structure-based drug design and integrating them with experimental workflows.
• 3 months at UCAM for chemical biology expertise
• 3 months at FUB for physics-based modelling
• 3 months at ARQ for deep learning methods in drug design
DC8: De novo design of new modulators of TDP-43 by few-shot deep learning (Mentors: Ana Martinez & Carmen Gil, CSIC, Spain)
Host: CSIC Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project targets the discovery of novel modulators of TDP-43, a key protein implicated in ALS, using conditional deep learning approaches. The aim is to design molecules from scratch that interact with multiple targets, leveraging generative AI to overcome small-data limitations and accelerate multi-target drug discovery.

Key objectives: • Develop conditional generative models for de novo design of multitarget TDP-43 modulators • Validate generated molecules through in silico ranking and synthetic feasibility checks • Assess compound penetration and TDP-43 localisation in cell cultures using immunohistochemistry • Evaluate TDP-43 function via qRT-PCR and efficacy in ALS cellular models
The candidate will also contribute to integrating AI-driven design workflows with experimental validation for ALS treatment strategies.
Planned secondments: • 4 months at IBM for ML expertise • 4 months at TUE for generative modelling • 4 months at ARQ for training in ML and chemical biology
📌 Enrolment: Doctoral degree at UCM 🔗 Learn more about the application HER E!
DC9: Few-shot learning for chemical reaction outcome prediction (Mentor: Philippe Schwaller, EPFL, Switzerland)

This PhD project addresses one of the main bottlenecks in drug discovery: predicting the outcome of chemical reactions. Using few-shot learning and deep learning approaches, the goal is to improve reactivity prediction in low-data regimes, enabling sustainable and efficient synthetic planning.
• Develop and evaluate novel few-shot learning models for reaction outcome prediction
• Investigate how prediction accuracy improves with data size and identify optimal architectures
• Integrate negative data (failed reactions) and historical data into training strategies
• Create open-source tools for interpretable and user-friendly ML applications in chemistry
The candidate will also contribute to applying these models in real-world scenarios and designing frameworks for model interpretability.
• 6 months at AZ to develop ML methods
• 3 months at BRFAA for experimental validation
• 3 months at BGU for few-shot learning tool development
DC10: Advanced methods for autonomous agents and multimodal models in chemical synthesis and discovery (Mentor: Teodoro Laino, IBM, Switzerland)

This PhD project will develop advanced multimodal models and autonomous agents to accelerate chemical synthesis and discovery. The research will integrate diverse data sources—such as spectral data, chemical structures, and reaction environments—into predictive frameworks, while enabling autonomous agents to tackle complex tasks in chemistry, including combinatorial optimisation and formal verification.
• Design multimodal models that fuse multiple data types for improved predictive accuracy
• Develop autonomous agents capable of recognising, formulating, and solving complex chemical problems
• Generate synthetic datasets to overcome experimental data limitations and enhance ML robustness
• Apply methodologies to synthesise novel compounds and identify biological applications
The candidate will also contribute to creating AI architectures for autonomous problem-solving and applying them to industrial and research domains.
• 6 months at TUE to customise AI architectures for synthetic chemistry tasks
• 3 months at ARQ to apply and co-develop new deep learning strategies
MiningBrines involves 19 highly talented doctoral candidates.

MiningBrines provides a unique opportunity for its 19 highly talented doctoral candidates (DCs) to pursue their PhDs within a dynamic European network. This initiative connects universities and industry partners across 32 institutions in 10 countries: Belgium, Croatia, France, Germany, Italy, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States.

MLCARE – Machine Learning Computational Advancements for peRsonalized mEdicine (HORIZON – MSCA – 2024 – DN – 101226456 – MLCARE)
Machine Learning Computational Advancements for peRsonalized mEdicine (HORIZON – MSCA – 2024 – DN – 101226456 – MLCARE)

Precision medicine represents a paradigm shift in healthcare, transitioning from generalized treatment strategies to highly personalized care. This transformation is driven by rapid advancements in digital technologies, which generate massive volumes of data from diverse sources, including genomic sequences , high-resolution imaging, wearable devices, and electronic health records (EHRs). However, despite an annual estimate of 50 petabytes of data generated per hospital , only a fraction is utilized effectively. Harnessing this untapped potential offers a transformative opportunity to uncover novel disease mechanisms and deliver more precise and effective therapeutic interventions.

The MLCare project seeks to revolutionize precision medicine by developing cutting-edge AI solutions that integrate genomic, clinical, and environmental data into holistic, multimodal patient representations. Through innovative approaches such as Foundation Models and advanced generative AI methods, MLCare will address critical challenges in processing complex, high-dimensional, and multimodal datasets. Emphasis will be placed on ensuring the trustworthiness , explainability, and security of AI applications to support real-world clinical decision-making.

A core mission of MLCare is to train a new generation of 14 interdisciplinary researchers with expertise spanning AI, computational biology, and healthcare . The program will equip doctoral candidates with the technical, analytical, and ethical skills needed to lead the future of patient-centered, AI-driven medicine. By combining state-of-the-art research with a comprehensive training program, MLCare aims to set new standards in personalized healthcare, ensuring equitable, data-driven solutions that improve outcomes across diverse populations. This project is poised to position Europe at the forefront of global innovation in precision medicine , delivering a timely and impactful response to evolving healthcare challenges.
